what_it_does: Serverless computing (also called Function-as-a-Service, or FaaS) lets cloud providers run small pieces of code on demand, but to prevent one customer's code from reading another's data, each function normally runs in its own isolated container or lightweight virtual machine — a strong but expensive boundary that takes milliseconds to set up and cross. Many modern microservices need to respond in microseconds, so that isolation overhead is a serious problem. Jord places multiple functions inside a single shared memory address space (the same memory map visible to one process) and instead uses fine-grained hardware memory protection — a mechanism that marks individual memory regions as off-limits to code that does not own them — to keep functions from touching each other's data. This avoids costly operating-system involvement on every call and lets functions pass data to each other by simply handing over a pointer rather than copying bytes, enabling microsecond-level response times.
